sessions.title: Your Calendar Is Your Ceiling
sessions.desc: You built the business to be free. Somewhere along the way it took the freedom. Vishen opens his own load map live, the years Mindvalley ran through him and what AI runs there today, then names the ceiling every founder shares: your business can't grow faster than your calendar.

sessions.title: Find Your 3 Biggest Time Drains
sessions.desc: Where do your hours actually go? Map your week live, rank where AI pays off, and leave with the three workflows to fix first, and the ones that should stay human.

sessions.title: What to Automate First
sessions.desc: Most founders try to automate everything at once and stall. Nate takes the three drains from the last session and shows how AI-native founders pick the first ones to hand over, and what those first automations look like running.

sessions.title: Your Voice, Made Executable
sessions.desc: A voice skill trained on your own words, not a template. One idea turned into a week of posts, emails and a page, with an anti-slop gate so nothing ships that sounds like AI.

sessions.title: From Idea to Launch in a Day

sessions.title: Find Where Your Clients Slip Away
sessions.desc: You don't have a lead problem. You have a leak problem. Attention, lead, follow-up, sale: this session maps the journey end to end with real funnels and real numbers from two decades at Mindvalley, so you know exactly where AI should go first.

survey.title: Help us build AI for Founders
survey.intro: About eight minutes, and most of it is writing, not ticking. In the quiz you told us what you want fixed: the business running beyond you, more leads, more done without hiring, and the question we heard most, what should I automate first. We have drafted the fix: sixteen weeks, eight modules. Before we decide who teaches what, we want to know whether we got it right. Your answers go to the people writing the curriculum, not to a dashboard. Version two is published with the changes marked, so you can see what moved because of you.
survey.method: The survey runs on Compassionate Curiosity, Kwame Christian's three-step frame for conversations where someone wants something: acknowledge and validate the feeling, get curious with compassion, then solve the problem together. Part one lets people name what the week feels like before we ask anything about us. Parts two to four ask open questions in a warm register, for stories and specifics rather than opinions. Part five turns the conversation into joint problem solving: what would need to be true in March, who should be in the room, and how far they want to go with us. People value what they help build, so the last part is the point, not an afterthought.

brief_map.how: Part one: who they are, what they sell, hours the business needs them, and a recent week in their own words (1 to 4).
Question 15, what would need to be true in March, and the first half of question 10, their own version of what should I automate first.
Questions 10 to 12 on the outline: exactly my problem or not how it is for me, what is nowhere in it, more of and skip. Recurring answers become the version two change log.
Question 3 (the week), question 8 (what still goes through them and which to lift first) and the module grid at question 9, read against the quiz's own weights.

brief_map.ask: What they do not know they should know.
brief_map.how: Asked directly at question 16, and surfaced by questions 5, 6 and 7, where the story of the last attempt and the tools that do not connect show the gap they cannot name.
Question 13, open: who they have learned most from, inside Mindvalley or outside, what works about how that person teaches, and who they would want in the room. No list, so nothing is promised.

brief_map.ask: Serves marketing as well as curriculum.
brief_map.how: Questions 3, 10 and 15 are the language bank for the summit and sales page; question 13 says which voices this audience trusts; question 17 builds the founding circle.
Five parts, programme-agnostic: your week, what you have tried, the outline, people and lines, building it together. Swap the module list and the outline and it runs for any Mastery.

sections.title: Part 1 · Your week
sections.lead: Three quick ones, then one that takes a minute.

questions.text: Which describes you best right now?
options: Solo founder: coach, consultant, practitioner or creator. The business is me.
Founder with a team of up to ten
Founder with a team of more than ten
Planning to start a business in the next year
questions.why: The quiz asked this too, but we ask again: it costs one tap, it may have changed, and it sets the wording of questions 3 and 8 and lets us read the pre-business quarter of the audience separately.

questions.text: What does your business mainly sell, or will it?
questions.why: The quiz did not ask. Decides which examples and skill packs we build first.

questions.text: Tell us about a recent week when everything came back to you. What happened, and how did you feel by Friday?

variants.team: Tell us about a recent week when everything came back to you. What happened, and what do you wish your team could have handled without you?
variants.planning: What is stopping you starting, and what would you need to see to begin?

questions.why: The first real question names the feeling before we ask for anything. For founders with a team the second half asks what the team could carry, because the quiz barely mentioned team and Module 6 needs the evidence. Pre-business founders get their own version.

questions.text: In a normal week, how many hours does your business need you personally to keep running?
questions.why: The before picture. The programme is measured against the founder load map, and this is its first rough reading across the community.

sections.title: Part 2 · What you have tried
sections.lead: No judgement here. Half the people who took the quiz have barely started, and that is exactly who this is for.

questions.text: Walk us through the last time you tried to hand something to AI, or to a person. What did you hope would happen, and what actually happened?
questions.why: A story, not an opinion. The gap between hoped and happened is the knowledge gap or the application gap, in their words.

questions.text: What has stopped you going further with AI in your business? Say it the way you would say it to a friend.
questions.why: The blocker, uncoded. Asking for the friend version lowers the guard and gets the real reason rather than the respectable one.

questions.text: Which tools would AI need to talk to in your business for this to be real? Name them.
questions.why: Integration was the loudest theme in the quiz and nobody was asked which tools. The answers set the connector list for Get AI-Ready and tell us where a lab will hit a wall.

questions.text: Which of these still have to go through you? Tick everything that applies, then tell us the one you would most like off your desk first.
options: Finding leads and following them up
Deciding what to build or sell next
questions.why: The eight options are the eight modules in plain words. The quiz gave us the weight by area at a coarser grain; the one pick here is the priority test for the module order. Solo founders see delegating to contractors or AI in place of hiring.

sections.title: Part 3 · The outline
sections.lead: Read the draft outline, shown here. Nothing in it is fixed.

questions.text: For each of the eight modules, how much do you need it?
questions.why: The one quantitative read on the outline. Four points, no midpoint. The share answering need it or urgently becomes each module's need index, by founder type.

questions.text: Module 1 is built to answer the question we heard most in the quiz: what should I automate first? Is that your question, or is yours different? Write it the way you would ask it. Then tell us where else in the outline you thought: that is exactly my problem, or, that is not how it is for me.
questions.why: Tests the opening module against the audience's own words, then reads the rest of the outline the same way. The first half gives marketing the hook; the second tells the curriculum where a lesson is framed for someone else.

questions.text: What problem in your business is nowhere in this outline?
questions.why: The gap question, asked as a problem rather than a topic. Recurring answers become the version two change log.

questions.text: What would you want more of, and what would you skip?
questions.why: Depth and cuts in one optional question. Sixteen weeks is long; this tells us where to spend and where to save.

sections.title: Part 4 · People, and lines
sections.lead: Two questions. No names are promised.

questions.text: Who have you learned the most from about running a business, with AI or without, inside Mindvalley or outside? What is it about how they teach that works for you, and is there anyone you would want in the room for this?
questions.why: Vishen's which teachers question, asked open so nobody is promised and names we have not thought of can surface. The how they teach half briefs every guest; the names go to the roster conversation, not to the page.

questions.text: What is the line you would never let AI cross in your business, and why?
questions.why: Data safety and authenticity were the two worries raised unprompted in the quiz. Asked as a line rather than a tick, it tells us where the human checkpoint has to sit in every lab, and gives Module 2 its governance examples.

sections.title: Part 5 · Building it together
sections.lead: The part that makes this a conversation rather than a form.

questions.text: If we built this together, what would need to be true in March for you to say the sixteen weeks were worth it?
questions.why: The promise in their words and timeframe. The quiz said the business running beyond me; this tells us what that looks like on a Tuesday in March, and the phrases become the sales page.

questions.text: What do you suspect you do not know yet, that a founder running on AI should know?
questions.why: Vishen's what they do not know they should know, asked directly. The unprogrammed worries the quiz could not reach.

questions.text: Would you like to be part of the founding circle that shapes version two?
options: Review version two before it is published
Join a 45-minute group call with the curriculum team
Not this time, just keep me posted
questions.why: The commitment question, with two real offers. Everyone who ticks either has put something in, and the list becomes the founding circle.

questions.text: May we follow up with you on your answers?
options: No, use my answers but do not contact me about them
questions.why: Consent, and where the email matches a quiz row, the join to that person's quiz answers.

survey.thanks: Thank you. Your answers go straight to the people writing the curriculum, and they are read in full. Version two of the outline is published on [date], with every change marked, so you can see what moved because of you. If you asked to join the founding circle you will hear from us within a week. The AI for Founders Summit runs 30 October to 1 November; your seat is saved at [link].
design_notes: Length: about eight minutes. Eighteen questions, eleven open, four optional (7, 12, 14, 16). The intro says most of it is writing, so people arrive expecting to type.

Nothing the quiz settled at population level is asked again except role, which is one tap and drives the branching. Revenue and biggest result are not asked; the quiz record is joined by email at question 18 where one exists.
Order follows Compassionate Curiosity: acknowledge (part 1), get curious (parts 2 to 4), build together (part 5). The feeling comes before any opinion about us; the commitment comes last.
Branching: question 1 sets the wording of question 3 (team, pre-business) and question 8 (solo). The outline is shown inline before question 9 so nobody leaves the form.
Open questions ask for a story or a specific, never a rating in words. Closed questions do two jobs only: segment (1, 2, 4) and one quantitative read on the outline (8, 9).
Incentive is recognition, not a prize: early sight of version two, and a 45-minute group call with the curriculum team. Nothing is tested on anyone and nobody is quoted.
No question about the time slot: it is set at 7am Pacific for team capacity. The invitation says live when you can, recording when you cannot.
Send on a Tuesday, remind on Friday to non-openers and partial completions only, close the following Tuesday.
Mobile first, progress shown. Typeform or an Airtable form; responses land in the AI for Founders base once Vishen has aligned, in a sheet until then.
analysis: Where an email matches a quiz row, join the two so revenue and the quiz's biggest result travel with the new answers without being asked again.

Open answers are read in full, not summarised. Questions 3, 5, 6, 10 and 15 are coded by hand into recurring themes; the phrases go into a language bank for lesson copy and the sales page. Hostile or off-topic answers (the quiz had a few) are routed, not counted.
Module need index: the share answering need it or need it urgently on question 9, by founder type, read against question 8 and the quiz's own weights (operations 33, marketing 26, sales 21 percent).
Gaps: questions 10 to 12 become the version two change log, with a rough count beside each change.
Connectors: question 7 produces the tool list for Get AI-Ready and flags the labs that will hit an integration wall.
Lines: question 14 sets where the human checkpoint sits in each lab and supplies Module 2's governance examples.
Teachers: question 13 yields names and teaching qualities. The qualities brief every guest; the names go to the roster conversation.
Founding circle: everyone who ticks an active option in question 17 goes on a list with their answers attached and sees version two first.
Version two is published with a change log that credits the survey: what moved, and roughly how many people asked for it.
quiz_insights: 907 people took the AI for Founders quiz; 747 wrote an answer to the open question. The second survey does not repeat what it settled.

Who they are is known at the population level: 62 percent solo founder or creator, 15 percent planning to start, 15 percent small team. Question 1 asks again, one tap, so the branching works for everyone, including people who never took the quiz.

What they most want to transform is known: operations and automation 33 percent, marketing 26 percent, sales 21 percent; finance 5 percent, team and hiring 1 percent. Module 6 is the one most at risk of a nice to have, so the team segment gets its own open question.
The biggest result they want is the business running beyond me (30 percent), ahead of more leads (27 percent). That is the promise line in their words; question 15 tests it.
The most repeated open answer, 23 times word for word, was what should I automate first. Module 1 is built for it; question 10 asks whether they recognise their question in it.
Integration was the loudest open theme (33 percent of answers): tools that do not connect, how to bring AI in safely and in order. The quiz never asked which tools; question 7 does.
Data safety (7 percent) and authenticity (5 percent, AI makes things polished and uniform) are the two worries people raised unprompted. Question 14 asks for the line they would never let AI cross.
Half the room has barely started: 19 percent not at all, 33 percent writing and ideas only. The story of the last attempt (question 5) matters more than any rating.
The quiz's one open question drew a median of 72 characters and 23 people typed the example back. It captured topics, not stories. This survey is the depth pass, which is why it is mostly open.

emails.body:
Hi [Name],

Expert & Authority Mastery sold out.

I want to say thank you before anything else. You came to the summit, you asked hard questions in the Q&A, you told us what you were building and what was in the way. The programme that's running right now was shaped by that. The curriculum came out of your survey answers before a single lesson was written. That's the only way I know how to build.

So here's what's next.

On 30 October to 1 November we're running a new, free, three-day event: the AI for Founders Summit.

It's not about learning AI. We already have a programme for that. This one is about the business. Specifically, the founder's problem nobody teaches: everything still runs through you. Every lead, every proposal, every client question, every decision waits for your hours. You built the business to be free and somewhere along the way it took the freedom. [Vishen: your own Mindvalley example here, two sentences, the one from the story interview.]

Over three days we'll show you what to automate first in your business, then build it live, step by step. The company brain. The lead that never goes cold. Content in your own voice.

Here's where you come in.

Back in 2015 we built a programme with our community instead of for it. We shared the rough outline, asked what was missing, and published the version they'd shaped. It was the best launch we'd ever done, and the programme was better for it.

I want to do that again. This week you'll get a short survey from us: where your business is, what eats your week, what you'd want a programme like this to fix first. Then we'll publish the curriculum for the summit and the Mastery, openly, before it's finished, and ask you what's missing.

[Photo: Vishen and Gareth, MVU or the KL office. Working, not posed. Group shot with Jaideep if one exists.]

The person reading your answers is Gareth Winter, our Head of Content and Creative Director. Gareth designs our curricula. He'll take what you tell us and publish version two of the programme with your input in it, so you can see exactly what changed because of you.

Save your seat here, and watch for the survey.

[Link: save my seat at the AI for Founders Summit]

Vishen

P.S. from Gareth: I read every answer, not a summary of them. The questions you asked in the Expert & Authority survey are already in this curriculum. Tell me what's missing, and you'll see it in the next version. Gareth
notes: Copy only, for Ramya to craft. Placeholders in brackets need a name, a link, the photo, or Vishen's own line.

Register: no exclamation marks, no formal connectives, one coined idea (co-create) used three times; the enemy is the inherited setup of the business, never the reader. Role credit for consistent use: Gareth Winter, Head of Content and Creative Director, designs Mindvalley's curricula.

basis: Version two, 14 October 2026. Built from Vykintas Glodenis's curriculum proposals (5 and 8 Oct), Jaideep's launch brief (5 Oct) and curriculum review (14 Oct), the AI for Founders quiz (907 submissions, 747 open answers), and the team call of 14 Oct with Marisha and Vykintas: start with the thing a customer sees, bring the company brain in once its absence is felt, pair every inspiring lesson with a step-by-step lab, structure the journey around the building blocks of a business, and level the room with an optional pre-recorded onboarding. Authors for guest lessons are mapped later.
pattern: The problem founders name in that pillar
The idea: how an AI-first founder thinks about it, taught in the Tuesday lesson, with the finished thing shown first
The system: a ready-made skill, template or workflow for that pillar, installed and adapted to each founder's business in the Thursday lab
What changes: something observable, running by Thursday night, listed on the Automation Hub with its owner

lab_format.title: Every lab runs the same way
steps: Ten minutes: the finished build shown again, and the three steps named
Sixty minutes: three timed builds of twenty minutes, each ending with a checkpoint screenshot in the thread (bending time is the rule)
Twenty minutes: unsticking, in two rooms, solo founders and founders with a team
Before the lab: a pre-recorded step-by-step twin, chaptered, and the template, so nobody is lost live
After the lab: one thing running, named on the Automation Hub with its owner and its checkpoint

onboarding.title: Get AI-Ready, optional and pre-recorded
onboarding.text: An evergreen sequence under two hours, updated as the tools change: your account and plan, one project with instructions, one skill installed, one app connected, and a short guide for people coming from ChatGPT. Optional, with a readiness checklist that nudges and never gates. Two live drop-in calls on 5 and 12 November for questions; nobody has to attend them. No minute of lesson one is spent on setup.

changelog: The order now follows a customer's journey through the business. Week 1 ships a website; the company brain moves to weeks 7 and 8, after six weeks of building have made its absence felt (team call, 14 Oct).
Lesson one is the wow: feed AI your business, find the offer, install the copy skill, drop the copy in and watch the site appear. The lab hosts it (Vykintas, 14 Oct).
Week 1 installs two reusable skills, copywriting and website building, so every later page, funnel and email is built with them (Vykintas, 14 Oct).

Week 2 is brand voice, then funnel: the voice pack improves the site and later seeds the brain; the funnel ends in a quiz, a calculator or a booked call, with the lead magnet and welcome sequence behind it (team call, 14 Oct).
Week 2 builds the lead magnet and a five-email welcome sequence: the first thing running unattended is in week 2, not week 10 (Jaideep's review).

Week 3 is short form, long form, lead form: articles on your own website answer what buyers ask so AI engines and search find you, then each article becomes carousels, posts, reels and a newsletter, and a month is scheduled (team call, 14 Oct; quiz: content is the solo founder's biggest time-eater).

Week 4 shows both routes to traffic, organic and one paid ad attached to a sale, and stops there: producing content is in scope, growing a following belongs to the social media Mastery (Marisha, 14 Oct).
The Monday page starts in week 8, three numbers the brain reports every Monday, so the week 14 dashboard has history (Jaideep's review).
Week 10 adds the Automation Hub page: every scheduled run in one list with its owner and checkpoint (Jaideep's review).
The week 14 dashboard recommends: do this, try this, spend time here (Jaideep's review).
Week 15 is the week you only decide: systems and owners run, the founder reviews. Reworded from a week without you, to keep the promise honest (Jaideep's review, our promise rule).
Week 16 is Demo Day, a showcase of one running system per module. The word certification is retired (product decision, 6 Oct).
The load map moves into the Monday opening as homework, so the before number exists before lesson one and no week is spent on it.
Every lab runs one fixed format with a pre-recorded twin, so inspiration on Tuesday never leaves a non-technical founder lost on Thursday (team call, 14 Oct).
Get AI-Ready becomes optional and pre-recorded, continuously updated, with two drop-in calls (team call, 14 Oct).
Vishen teaches three sessions: the opening, week 14 and the graduation. Guest lessons are unassigned until the team maps authors.
The builder track (PRD, ship your own software) stays out of the sixteen weeks; app-building belongs to AI Mastery.

modules.name: Module 1: Your front door
modules.problem: Nobody can find me, or buy from me, without me explaining it.
modules.installed: Two reusable skills, copywriting and website building; the Founder Context Pack (your starter brain); your offer on one page; a live website in your words with editorial photos; your brand voice pack; a funnel (a landing page with proof, a quiz, calculator or booking link, a lead magnet and a welcome sequence) that runs on its own.
modules.changes: The business has a front door and a funnel that capture and welcome people while the founder sleeps, every word in the founder's voice, and the founder has fed AI their business once, the way everything else here gets built.

modules.name: Module 2: Marketing engine
modules.problem: Nobody is finding me, and content eats my time.
modules.installed: The content engine: short form, long form, lead form. Articles on your website that answer what buyers ask, so AI engines and search find you; one long piece turned into a month of carousels, posts, reels and emails; one ad attached to a sale; your channels pointed at the funnel; a signal dashboard.
modules.changes: People find the founder without being told where to look, a month of content in the founder's voice is scheduled, and demand shows on a dashboard before anything is sold.

modules.name: Module 3: Sales
modules.installed: Lead research, qualification and follow-up skills; proposals from your assets; call prep and debrief; a pipeline view; one channel test running.
modules.changes: Every lead answered within the hour and followed up; the founder takes only the calls that need them.

modules.name: Module 4: Company brain
modules.problem: Six weeks of assets in six places; AI gives generic answers; the team keeps asking the founder.
modules.installed: Everything built so far in one governed place: offers, customers, voice, numbers, processes and decisions; data rules; pipelines that keep it current; the Monday page.
modules.changes: Every later system, and every team member, works from one source, and three numbers arrive every Monday.

modules.name: Module 5: Operations and delivery
modules.problem: Client work and questions land on the founder.
modules.installed: Client onboarding flow; processes turned into skills; first-line support drafts; scheduled check-ins; inbox and invoice triage; the Automation Hub page.
modules.changes: Routine client work runs from the system; the founder reviews rather than does; Monday starts with a report.

modules.name: Module 6: Team: people and AI

modules.changes: Solo: contractors plus AI instead of a first hire. Team: new people productive in days.

notes: Version two, 14 October: the order now follows a customer’s journey through the business (front door, marketing, sales, then the company brain in weeks 7 and 8, operations, team, finance, product), lesson one builds a website live, every lab runs one fixed format with a pre-recorded twin, Get AI-Ready is optional and pre-recorded, and Week 16 is Demo Day. Built from the team call of 14 October (Marisha, Vykintas), Jaideep’s curriculum review, Vykintas’s proposals of 5 and 8 October and the quiz. Guest lessons are unassigned until the team maps authors; the full list of changes is on the outline page.

Rebuilt on 5 October from three sources: Vykintas Glodenis’s curriculum proposal (eight modules, one business pillar each, the problem / management idea / installed system / observable change pattern, and the Get AI-Ready onboarding layer), Jaideep’s launch brief (16 weeks from Monday 16 November, two sessions per module, the summit on 30 October to 1 November), and the AI for Founders quiz (812 answers: operations, marketing and sales are where the pain is; solo founders start with marketing, founders with teams with operations; data safety and sounding like me are the unprogrammed worries).

Team direction, 26 September (Jaideep, Marijana, Marta): Vishen leads the summit and takes only the big Mastery sessions; Vykintas leads the Mastery curriculum and every implementation lab; roughly one guest teacher per pillar; at least one more woman on the roster. Every guest here is placed where they are most authentic, from the names in consideration on 5 October, and none is confirmed for the Mastery until the team says so.

Cadence, decided 5 October, hour set 7 October: Tuesday lesson, Thursday lab, 7am Pacific (3pm London; 2pm London in the final week), Tuesday 17 November 2026 to Thursday 18 March 2027, with a break from 21 December to 3 January. Expert & Authority runs Tuesday and Friday; this programme deliberately does not match it. Vykintas leads every lab here and already holds 8 of Expert & Authority’s Friday workshops at 9am Pacific inside this run (20 Nov, 27 Nov, 18 Dec, 8 Jan, 29 Jan, 5 Feb, 12 Feb, 19 Feb), so a Friday lab would put him in two rooms on the same morning on each of those dates.

The opening is Monday 16 November, the start date in the brief, with Vishen. It also keeps him clear of his Expert & Authority lesson at the same hour on Tuesday 17 November once the John Lee rotation is applied.

Thanksgiving, decided 5 October and checked against the day on 7 October: the Week 2 lab stays on Thursday 26 November, Thanksgiving Day in the US. Expert & Authority’s 2025 reading was that the week holds, and it kept its Friday 27 November workshop. The 2025 Mastery records confirm the week and sharpen the day: AI Mastery’s sessions the day before (422 against 454 and 447 the Wednesdays either side) and the day after (307 against 274 and 313) showed no dip; the one session that ran on Thanksgiving Day itself, Entrepreneurship Mastery’s Thursday lesson, kept 214 of a usual 300, about 70 percent, and its recording was watched more that week than any other Thursday’s that month. So the lab runs, Vykintas-led and recorded, and the Tuesday 1 December lesson picks up anyone who missed it. Wednesday 25 November is the alternative if the team prefers not to run on the day; the day before showed no dip.

Time slot, set 7 October: 7am Pacific, which is 3pm London for every week but the last and 2pm London on 16 and 18 March 2027 (US clocks change on 14 March, UK clocks on 28 March). Janja set the hour for team capacity and schedule; the data supports it. Attendance across five Mastery bases shows no hour effect between 7am and 10am Pacific (Entrepreneurship Mastery moved from 5pm to 3pm London mid-cohort and attendance did not move), Manifesting and Speaking & Influence Mastery run at 3pm London with the highest live rates in the set, and the final hour-by-hour preference was for 9am because about 60 percent of students are in North America; that was never a hill to die on. Students are told the Pacific time; London is the derived time. Evidence in briefs/AIF-TIME-SLOT-EVIDENCE.md.

What this programme leaves to AI Mastery: how models work, prompting in depth, image and video generation, writing skills from scratch, building apps. Where both touch the same tool the angle differs: the brain in AI Mastery is your personal knowledge; here it is the company’s, shared with the team. Neither is the advanced one.

Outside the modules there are only three sessions, all before Week 1: Get AI-Ready calls 1 and 2, which are Vykintas’s and in his proposal as written (the content of each call is a first pass), and the Monday opening with Vishen, the kickoff from the earlier draft moved to the start date in the brief. Office hours and an alumni reunion were in the earlier draft and were removed on 7 October: Vishen’s diary cannot carry extra calls, and what happens after graduation is a separate conversation, not part of the Mastery. Expert & Authority’s own Airtable holds only lessons, workshops, one bonus and the graduation.

Summit learnings applied: a live build directly before every offer; every session leaves something built; written topic lock for every Vishen session two weeks ahead and no previews of unreleased tools; a sound check at every speaker handoff; untested builders get a paid webinar or Highlights slot before the summit; Shawn never follows Vykintas in the same event.

sessions.title: Why Your Business Still Runs on You
sessions.description: The programme opens on Monday 16 November with Vishen. You built the business to be free; somewhere along the way it took the freedom. Vishen opens his own load map live: the years Mindvalley ran through him, and what AI runs there today. Then the ceiling every founder in the room shares: your business cannot grow faster than your calendar. Vykintas walks the sixteen weeks and the one measurement Demo Day is judged against: how many hours a week your business needs you today. He also sets the rule every lab runs on: bending time, three timed builds of twenty minutes, a checkpoint after each. Homework before lesson one: your load map and your before number, so no week is spent on it. You leave with the calendar in your hands, a number written down, and a website due on Thursday.

sessions.title: Feed AI Your Business. Watch It Build Your Website.
sessions.description:
The finished thing first. A founder's website built live, in the opening ten minutes, from a two-minute voice note and three documents, before any teaching. Then the one idea every week after this runs on: AI is only as good as what you feed it, and you are about to feed it your whole business.

Four steps, shown and installed, not taught to depth: the Founder Context Pack (who you serve, what you sell, what customers say, your proof, ten minutes of you talking, transcribed), which is the starter brain that week 7 formalises; the Offer Finder, which interrogates the pack and returns three offers so one can be chosen and written as promise, format and price; the copywriting skill, run against the pack through an anti-slop gate so the page sounds like you; and the website-building skill, where the copy goes in and your business appears on a screen. Both skills are yours to keep: whenever you need copy or a page again, they are covered. Two tracks from the first minute: solo and pre-business founders choose their offer, founders with a team sharpen the one they already sell.

Homework before Thursday: send the preview to one real customer and ask one question. The win is the idea in your head on a page you did not have on Monday, and the knowledge that you built it.
sessions.brief: The finished thing first: a founder's site built live from a two-minute voice note. Then the one idea the whole programme runs on: AI is only as good as what you feed it, so you feed it your business once, in a Founder Context Pack, and it finds your offer, writes your page in your voice, and builds the site. Two skills are installed on the way, copywriting and website building, and you keep both for every page you ever need again. Both impressive and fundamental: this is context engineering, learned by doing.

sessions.title: Your Site, Live by Thursday
sessions.description:
Three timed builds. Twenty minutes: the copy polished with the customer's reaction, the anti-slop pass, the offer's price and format fixed. Twenty minutes: the site generated and hosted, the domain connected; the template picks the host, so this is clicks, not configuration. Twenty minutes: your own photos turned into editorial shots for the site, and email capture with a thank-you page wired and a test signup sent; the things you thought would cost money are now free. Then unsticking in two rooms. The URL goes in the community thread: thirty live sites in one thread is the proof the cohort is real.

**The win:** Your business has a front door, and you built it

sessions.title: Your Brand Voice, Then Your Funnel
sessions.description:
A website nobody captures from is a brochure. Before the funnel, the voice: a brand voice pack written from your own words (how you sound, what you never say, your story, your visual rules), so every page, email and post from here reads as one person. It is the first thing that goes into the company brain in week 7, and it improves the site you built last week.

Then the funnel, built with the copywriting and website-building skills from week 1: a landing page with your testimonials and proof, a quiz, calculator or book-a-call step matched to what you sell (most founders in the room sell a service, so most funnels end in a booked call), the lead magnet that earns an email (a scorecard, a checklist, a short assessment, generated from the Context Pack), and the five-email welcome sequence that does the first conversations in your voice. Shown first: a founder's funnel taking a booking while they are on stage.

The idea underneath: every asset is written once, saved as a skill, and reused everywhere. Two tracks: solo founders build the funnel around the offer; founders with a team wire it to the list and tools they already have. Once the funnel exists, traffic has somewhere to go, which is what weeks 3 and 4 are for.
sessions.brief: A site nobody captures from is a brochure. First the brand voice pack: how everything you send sounds and looks, written once from your own words, and later the first thing that goes into your company brain. Then the funnel built on last week's two skills: a landing page with your proof, a quiz, a calculator or a booking link, the lead magnet that earns an email, and the welcome sequence that does the first five conversations for you. The first system in your business that works while you sleep.

The funnel page generated with the two skills, the quiz or booking step wired to it, and the lead magnet placed behind the signup. The five-email welcome sequence written from the Context Pack, through the anti-slop gate, scheduled, and tested end to end; then the first entry on your Automation Hub: what runs, when, who owns it, where the checkpoint is. sessions.title: Short Form, Long Form, Lead Form
sessions.description:
How one person now matches the output of a marketing team, and why it starts with the website you already built. Long form first: articles on your site that answer the questions and objections your buyers actually ask, written by AI from the Context Pack in your brand voice. This is AEO, answer engine optimisation, search for the AI age: when someone asks an AI who to hire, those articles are how it finds you and why it calls you the authority. Short form second: every article is the source for carousels, posts, reels, a newsletter and scripts, cut in seconds, so the narrative is written once and travels everywhere. Lead form third: every piece points at the funnel from week 2.

Content is the solo founder's biggest time-eater in the quiz, and sounding like a robot is the most repeated worry; this is the week both stop. The idea: a system that produces a month, not a founder who produces a post. This is one lesson on producing content, not a social media programme; growing a following is a different Mastery.
sessions.brief: How people find you now: AI engines answer their questions, and the answers come from articles on your website. The content engine in three layers: long form (articles that answer what your buyers ask, written by AI from your Context Pack, so search and AI find you), short form (each article cut into carousels, posts, reels and a newsletter in seconds), lead form (every piece pointing at the funnel). The week content stops eating the founder's time.

sessions.description:

One article turned into carousels, posts, reels and a newsletter, and the ten-second version saved as a skill so every future article does the same. A month scheduled before the lab ends, each piece pointing at the funnel, and the run listed on the Automation Hub.

**The win:** People can find you, and a month of content is scheduled

sessions.title: From Content to Demand
sessions.description: Content nobody captures is a hobby. The traffic layer, both routes shown: organic, which platform is your front door and how the content engine from week 3 fills it; and paid, one ad built from an article, attached to a sale, and run through AI connected to your ad account, so the ad manager is a conversation, not a dashboard. Most founders in the room will prefer organic because ads cost money; both are shown so the choice is theirs. Then the signals that tell you demand is real before you spend a week building the thing. The idea: marketing's second half is not more content, it is a list that grows while you work, and a dashboard that says whether it is.
sessions.brief: Content nobody captures is a hobby.
